extras.title: Abu’l-Khayr’s Uzbek steppe realm
extras.note: A post-Horde steppe realm; not the modern state of Uzbekistan or all Uzbek communities.

extras.title: Kazakh khanate and zhuzes
extras.note: Kerei and Janibek established a khanate after migration into Moghulistan. Later zhuzes had distinct, overlapping political paths.

extras.title: Bukhara and Transoxiana · khanate eras
extras.note: Shibanid, Janid and early Manghit arrangements are grouped; capitals, borders and the location of effective authority changed.

extras.title: Emirate of Bukhara
extras.location: Parts of present-day Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and neighbouring countries
extras.note: Manghit emirate; Russian domination after 1868 did not immediately abolish the emir’s government.

extras.title: Khwarazm / Khanate of Khiva
extras.note: Founded by a separate Jochid dynasty; not an offshoot of modern Uzbekistan or an ethnically uniform state.

extras.title: Khanate of Kokand
extras.note: A Fergana-based khanate whose expansion included diverse settled and nomadic communities.

extras.title: Russian rule in Central Asia
extras.note: A regional overview of annexed territories and unequal protectorates, not one uniform administration.

extras.title: Central Asia · revolution and early Soviet governments

extras.title: Moghulistan · eastern Chagataid realms
extras.location: Ili, Tian Shan and Tarim regions
extras.note: The eastern Chagataid political world continued after Timur’s rise in the west; rule later divided into regional branches.

extras.title: Yarkent Khanate
extras.note: One eastern Chagataid realm, with power increasingly contested by Khoja lineages and regional lords.

extras.title: Turpan · Chagataid and later oasis rule
extras.note: A selected regional frame; Chagataid rulers, local leaders and Dzungar overlords were distinct phases.

extras.title: Tarim Khoja governments under Dzungar supremacy
extras.note: Competing Sufi lineages ruled or influenced oasis governments; Dzungar khans demanded tribute and hostages.

extras.title: Dzungar Khanate
extras.location: Dzungaria and expanding Inner Asian territories
extras.note: An Oirat Mongol state, distinct from Chagataid realms. Qing conquest destroyed its government and devastated its population.

connections.label: 1991 · four independent states
connections.summary: The Soviet breakup left Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and Moldova as independent states.
connections.note: One geographic subset of the same union-wide breakup; the regional grouping is a viewing aid, not an intervening state. No present-day territorial claims are inferred.

connections.label: 1990–91 · independence restored
connections.summary: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania restored independence during the Soviet crisis.
connections.note: Soviet forces occupied and annexed these states in 1940. Lithuania proclaimed restoration in 1990; full independence and wider recognition followed in 1991. These are three of the fifteen final union republics.

connections.label: 1991 · three independent states
connections.summary: Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia became independent as Soviet authority broke down.
connections.note: One geographic subset of the same union-wide breakup; the regional grouping is a viewing aid, not an intervening state. No present-day territorial claims are inferred.

maps.title: Central Asia · khanates, Russian expansion and Soviet rule

connections.label: 1400s · eastern steppe powers
connections.summary: Abu’l-Khayr consolidated an Uzbek realm in the eastern Jochid steppe.
connections.note: One regional formation within post-Horde politics; other khanates and communities followed separate paths.

connections.label: 1460s · Kazakh khanate emerges
connections.summary: Kerei and Janibek left Abu’l-Khayr’s political orbit and founded a separate khanate.
connections.note: The conventional 1465 date marks consolidation, not the beginning of Kazakh people or all later territory.

connections.label: 1460s · refuge in Moghulistan
connections.summary: Kerei, Janibek and their followers settled in Moghulistan before consolidating their khanate.
connections.note: A political refuge and regional relationship, not the entire Moghulistan realm becoming Kazakhstan.

connections.label: 1500s · a Jochid dynastic link
connections.summary: Abu’l-Khayr’s grandson Muhammad Shaybani led conquests in Transoxiana.
connections.note: Dynastic connection and military expansion, not a simple renaming or migration of an entire state.

connections.label: 1500–12 · Uzbek conquests
connections.summary: Shaybani and subsequent Uzbek rulers defeated Timurid claimants and consolidated Transoxiana.
connections.note: Different cities changed hands repeatedly; Timurid dynastic histories continued in the Mughal realm.

connections.label: 1785 · Manghit emirate
connections.summary: Shah Murad’s rule marks the conventional emirate frame after Manghit consolidation.
connections.note: A change in ruling arrangements within Bukhara, not the creation of a new population.

connections.label: 1500s–1800s · neighbours and rivals
connections.summary: Bukhara and Khwarazm maintained separate ruling houses and competing regional interests.
connections.note: Contact does not imply that Khiva broke away from Bukhara or that either matches one modern nation.

connections.label: 1700s · Fergana consolidation
connections.summary: Fergana’s growing autonomy developed into the Kokand khanate.
connections.note: Separation and consolidation occurred in stages; the conventional 1709 foundation is not a sudden border-wide transfer.

connections.label: 1700s–1800s · Russian encroachment
connections.summary: Russian authority expanded through the Kazakh steppe by unequal agreements, administrative changes and conquest.
connections.note: Different zhuzes and regions were incorporated at different times, amid resistance.

connections.label: 1860s–76 · conquest and annexation
connections.summary: Russian forces took Kokandian territories and abolished the remaining khanate in 1876.
connections.note: Kokand’s dissolution did not end Kyrgyz, Uzbek, Tajik or other regional communities.

connections.label: 1868 · Russian domination
connections.summary: Bukhara came under Russian domination while retaining its emir’s government.
connections.note: This was unequal subordination and territorial loss, not immediate annexation of the whole emirate.

connections.label: 1873 · Khivan protectorate
connections.summary: Russian conquest reduced Khiva to a protectorate and annexed part of its territory.
connections.note: The khan’s restricted government survived until 1920.

connections.label: 1920 · khanate governments fall
connections.summary: Red Army campaigns and local revolutionary movements overthrew the Khivan khan and Bukharan emir.
connections.note: New Khorezm and Bukharan republics preceded later Soviet territorial reorganisation; armed resistance continued.

connections.label: 1924–36 · five union republics
connections.summary: Soviet reorganisation established Uzbek and Turkmen republics, followed by Tajik, Kazakh and Kyrgyz union republics.
connections.note: Tajikistan had an earlier autonomous status within Uzbekistan; Kazakh and Kyrgyz republics attained union status in 1936. This did not invent the region’s peoples.

connections.label: 1917 onward · revolution and war
connections.summary: Revolution broke imperial authority, followed by competing autonomy projects, civil war and Soviet consolidation.
connections.note: A regional overview of contested transitions, not the entire empire becoming one Soviet administration at once.

maps.title: Eastern Chagatai · Moghulistan, Tarim and Qing conquest

connections.label: 1340s · eastern khanate
connections.summary: Moghulistan emerged as the eastern Chagataid political realm while western power fragmented.
connections.note: Timur’s later western conquests did not eliminate the eastern Chagataid realm.

connections.label: 1500s · regional Chagataid branches
connections.summary: Chagataid rulers maintained distinct centres in the Tarim Basin and Turpan.
connections.note: Selected related branches after prolonged division and warfare; their territories did not comprise all former Moghulistan.

connections.label: 1670s · Khoja and Dzungar intervention
connections.summary: Afaq Khoja gained power in Kashgaria with Dzungar support, displacing Chagataid authority.
connections.note: Dating varies around 1678–1680; rival lineages and nominal princes continued to complicate local rule.

connections.label: 1670s–1750s · Dzungar supremacy
connections.summary: Dzungar khans imposed tribute and hostages on the Tarim Khoja governments.
connections.note: Overlordship and intervention, not the formation of the Dzungar state from the Chagataid dynasty.

connections.label: 1720s–50s · Qing alliance and rule
connections.summary: Turpan leaders sought Qing support against Dzungar power as Qing troops entered the oasis.
connections.note: Alliance, warfare, forced movement and later return unfolded over decades; Turpan was not simply annexed once in 1720.

connections.label: 1750s · Dzungar state destroyed
connections.summary: Qing campaigns destroyed the Dzungar state and incorporated its territories.
connections.note: The conquest brought catastrophic loss of life and displacement; surviving Oirat communities did not disappear.

connections.label: 1759 · Kashgaria conquered
connections.summary: Qing forces ended the Khojas’ government in Kashgaria.
connections.note: Resistance and Khoja political claims continued later; conquest did not end the region’s Muslim or Turkic communities.

researchNotes.scope: All fifteen final Soviet union republics represented across four regional views; existing Russia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan IDs reused. Seven additional Central Asian histories support the once-terminal Chagatai branch. No current international borders or territorial claims are drawn.
researchNotes.caution: The Bush Library finding-aid introduction gives a conflicting 31 December dissolution date; do not use it for the exact terminal date. It is used only to verify the fifteen state names. NATO and UN sources support 26 December, while the map deliberately uses the year 1991.
